tagline.text: Bohol's oldest church, built from coral stone

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half day to a full day

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,500 per person (for half a day)

image.credit: Philip Nalangan / CC BY 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A church built of coral stone in 1727 in Baclayon, where Jesuit missionaries founded Bohol's first Christian settlement in 1596. Its facade and bell tower, destroyed in the 2013 earthquake, have been restored and reopened, and together with the church museum in the old convent building, it's a beloved first stop on Bohol countryside tours.
Baclayon Church's official name is the Immaculate Conception Parish Church. It stands by the sea in Baclayon, about
6–7km
along the east coast road from Bohol's capital, Tagbilaran. In
November 1596
, Jesuit priests Juan de Torres and Gabriel Sanchez established a mission station here, making Baclayon the oldest Christian settlement in Bohol; it was elevated to a parish in
, and today's stone church was completed in

The church was built by stacking blocks of coral stone quarried from the sea and binding them with plaster mixed from lime and sand — and, according to legend, egg whites were mixed in to strengthen the bond. The square bell tower also served as a watchtower against pirates and raiding ships. Left unfinished when the Jesuits were expelled in
, it was completed in
by the Augustinian Recollects who took over the parish afterward. The church was declared a National Historical Landmark in
and a National Cultural Treasure in
, and as one of the Jesuit churches of the Philippines it's also on UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List.
The magnitude-7.2 earthquake that struck Bohol on
October 15, 2013

brought down the front portico and part of the bell tower. Restoration then proceeded under national government oversight, with each fallen stone numbered and put back in place, and the church reopened in
. Comparing it with pre-earthquake photos, you can spot where newly cut stones mix with the old ones — the traces of restoration are an attraction in themselves.
Inside are three gilded 18th–19th-century altar retablos and a pipe organ built in

, and the second floor of the adjoining convent building houses the church museum. Most Bohol countryside tours to Chocolate Hills, Loboc River, and the tarsiers start here, so you'll likely stop by even without planning to, but travelers interested in history and architecture should leave plenty of time to explore the museum unhurried.

Look closely at the mottled gray-and-white coral-stone walls and you can still see the shapes of shells and coral. The tower beside the church, part watchtower and part bell tower, is a relic of the days when it kept watch over the coast.

The retablos of the central and side altars date to the 18th and 19th centuries, and their gold leaf glows softly under candlelight and lighting. The interior, set off by a black-and-white checkerboard floor, photographs beautifully.
On the second floor of the old convent building, vestments, ivory saint statues, silver liturgical items, and records from the Jesuit mission era are on display. Admission is about
, and photography is not allowed inside the museum.
The pipe organ in the choir loft is one of the oldest surviving organs in the Philippines. If you're lucky, you can hear it played during Mass or a special recital.

Check the historical marker and before-and-after earthquake photos at the entrance, then look at the wall to spot where the color of the newly filled stones differs from the original ones. It's a fascinating experience for travelers interested in heritage restoration.

blocks.title: A seaside walk and old houses

children.text: Cross the road in front of the church and there's a seaside promenade, and the town still has wooden houses from the late Spanish era, making for a good short stroll through its lanes.
Baclayon's port is where bancas depart for Pamilacan Island, famous for dolphin watching. An itinerary that visits the church after an early-morning dolphin tour also works well.

Tour vehicles usually stay in Baclayon for only 30 minutes to an hour. If you want to see the museum too, tell your driver in advance so you get enough time.
From Manila to Bohol–Panglao International Airport (TAG) takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
. From the airport to Baclayon, via Tagbilaran city, is about
20km
, roughly
30–40 minutes
by car.
From Cebu, a fast craft like OceanJet takes about
2 hours
to Tagbilaran port (around
). From Tagbilaran port to Baclayon Church is about
7km
, reachable in about
15–20 minutes
by tricycle or Grab.
Jeepneys and multicabs heading toward Loay, Loboc, or Jagna, departing from Dao Integrated Bus Terminal or in front of Island City Mall in Tagbilaran, pass through central Baclayon. It takes about
15–20 minutes
, with fares around
— just ask to be let off in front of the church.
From Tagbilaran, a taxi or Grab costs about
. Countryside tour vehicles departing from Alona Beach on Panglao run about
per vehicle, and most include Baclayon Church as the first stop. Chartering a tricycle for half a day costs about
The church can be visited year-round, but
December
through
May
, when rain is scarce and skies are clear, is best for exterior photos and for combining the visit with the nearby seaside and Chocolate Hills. In
March–May
, midday temperatures climb to
and the churchyard gets hot, so it's better to visit in the morning.
From
June
to
November
is the rainy season with frequent afternoon showers, and in some years typhoons pass through in
October–December
. Since the church can still be toured indoors when it rains, it's a good stop to keep on a rainy-season itinerary. Around the feast of its patroness on
December 8
, the town holds a lively festival and procession, though Mass and events may limit viewing. Time-wise, avoid
when tour vehicles crowd in, and visit right after opening or after
3 PM
for a quieter experience.

Baclayon has a few small resorts and guesthouses by the sea, but most travelers stay on the beach resort island of Panglao or in Tagbilaran city, which is easy to get around from, and visit for half a day. Business hotels in Tagbilaran run about
a night; around Alona Beach on Panglao, guesthouses run about
and beach resorts about
. If you're planning an early-morning Pamilacan Island dolphin tour, staying at a place along the Baclayon coast is also an option.

For food, many travelers rely on the Loboc River cruise's buffet lunch or a restaurant in Tagbilaran city. Bohol's signature snacks include calamay, a chewy sticky-rice sweet served in a coconut-shell cup, peanut kisses shaped like Chocolate Hills, and desserts made from Bohol's purple ube yam — all popular as gifts. Being a coastal town, you can also try grilled fish and squid, and kinilaw, fish cured in vinegar.
The church is generally open from about
8 AM
to around
5 PM
, and the museum sometimes closes for lunch (around
), so it's best to go early in the morning.
The church is an active place of worship, so avoid sleeveless tops and short shorts, and it helps to bring a light cover-up for your shoulders.
Avoid touring or photographing the interior while Mass is in progress, and check the Mass schedule posted at the entrance.
Photography is banned inside the museum, but you can quietly take photos inside the church. It's polite not to use flash.
Countryside tours often visit Baclayon first, so leaving before
8 AM
lets you arrive ahead of the group tours.
The donation box and souvenir stall near the entrance help maintain the church, so even a small contribution supports the preservation of this heritage site.
Combined with a Pamilacan Island dolphin tour, a natural day plan is to depart Baclayon's port at dawn, return in late morning, and then visit the church.
As a National Cultural Treasure and an active place of worship, don't enter the altar area, touch the walls or sacred objects, or fly a drone without permission.
On days with weddings, funeral Masses, or feast-day events, viewing hours may be shortened or interior access restricted.
The coastal road in front of the church carries a lot of traffic, so be careful not to step back into it while taking photos.
Museum admission and opening hours can change depending on the parish, so check the on-site signage.
Souvenir shops or restaurants recommended by your tour driver can be pricier, so check prices in advance.
The churchyard sun is strong at midday, so bring a hat and water.
